opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the picture behind that idea is a kind of pie chart: there's a genetic slice and an environmental slice, and once you've made the environment "good enough," the environmental slice shrinks and whatever variation is left over must be genetic. That picture is just wrong about how development works.

Genes and environments don't add together. They interact all the way down. The classic example is a plant: you can have genetically different seeds, and which one grows taller depends entirely on the soil it's planted in. Put them in different soil and the ranking flips. So the question "how much of the height is genetic?" doesn't really have an answer, because it depends on the particular range of environments you happened to sample.

Heritability is a statistic about variation in a particular population in a particular set of circumstances. It isn't a measure of how fixed or determined a trait is. Height is highly heritable, and yet average height changed dramatically over a few generations because nutrition changed. High heritability tells you very little about what would happen if you changed the environment in some new way.

The deeper point, especially for human beings, is that there isn't a single dimension called "good enough environment" that you reach and then stop. Human environments are open-ended, and we're constantly creating new ones. That's what culture is. Each generation of children grows up in a world that previous generations made, and children are extraordinarily good at learning from and adapting to whatever that world turns out to be. That plasticity is arguably the most distinctive thing about our species. A long, protected childhood exists precisely so that we can respond to environments that evolution never anticipated.

So the idea that once you've checked some boxes (enough food, no abuse, decent schools) the rest is written in the genes ignores the fact that the space of possible environments is enormous and largely unexplored. We don't know what a child would become in an environment nobody has invented yet. Looking at the variation in the environments we currently have, and concluding that's the limit, is a bit like studying plants in three kinds of soil and declaring you've learned everything about how plants can grow.

r001.rationale: The response describes gene–environment interactions and developmental plasticity generally, but does not connect the complexity of development to inconsistent genetic relationships with educational attainment or similar outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the argument goes something like this: if you equalize the environment, then the remaining variation has to be genetic, so heritability goes up and we conclude the trait is "really" genetic. And there's a sense in which that's just arithmetic. But I think it smuggles in a picture of development that's wrong, and I think the developmental biology and the developmental psychology both tell against it.

The first thing is that "good enough" is doing an enormous amount of work in that sentence. Good enough for what? Environments aren't a single dial that goes from bad to good. Human beings are the species that has the longest childhood of any animal, and I think the reason for that is precisely that we're designed to be shaped by variation in our environments, not to converge on a single outcome once the nutrition is adequate. If you look at the kinds of things that matter for children, it's not just calories and the absence of lead paint. It's who's talking to you, what language, what tools are lying around, what the people around you care about, what counts as a problem worth solving. Those vary enormously even across what we'd all agree are perfectly good middle-class homes, and they vary in ways that are very hard to measure with the kinds of instruments that behavior geneticists use.

The second thing is that heritability estimates are population-specific and they're statements about variance, not about mechanism. The classic example — if everyone in a society smokes, lung cancer looks highly heritable. That doesn't mean smoking stopped mattering. So when you say traits become "genetically determined" in good environments, what you really have is a statement that within that particular range of environments, the environmental differences you happened to measure don't account for much of the variance. That's a very different claim from saying the trait is fixed by the genes, and the slide from one to the other is where I think people go wrong.

And the third thing, which I find most interesting as a developmental psychologist, is that the whole genes-versus-environment framing assumes you can partition the causes additively. But what children actually do is actively construct their own environments. A curious child seeks out novelty, which makes her more curious, which changes which genes get expressed in the brain, and so on. Development is a cascade, not a sum. Once you have those kinds of feedback loops, the question "how much is genes and how much is environment" is a little like asking how much of the area of a rectangle is due to its length. You can ask it about a population of rectangles, but it tells you nothing about how rectangles work.

So my skepticism isn't that genes don't matter — of course they do. It's that the picture of a trait as something that's sitting there waiting to be revealed once you strip away the noise of bad environments is just not what development looks like from the inside. Caregiving, culture, the strange experimental intelligence of four-year-olds — those aren't noise. They're the mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response describes development as complex and interactive, but it does not mention inconsistent relationships between genetics and traits such as educational attainment or attribute that lack of consistency to developmental complexity.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the problem is that “good enough” assumes there’s some fixed range of environments, and once you get into that range, the environment stops making a difference. But that’s precisely what we don’t know. An environment can be perfectly good in the sense that children are well fed and loved and still differ enormously in what it allows them to learn and become.

And heritability is always relative to the particular environments you’re looking at. If everybody has a very similar environment, then differences between people will look more genetic. That doesn’t tell you what would happen if you changed the environment, especially in a way that falls outside the range you’ve studied.

Think about literacy. You can have a rich, flourishing human life in a society without writing, but you’re not going to learn to read. In a society where everyone goes to school, differences in reading ability might be substantially heritable. It would still be a mistake to conclude that the environment has ceased to matter.

So I don’t doubt that genes matter. I doubt that we can identify a threshold beyond which environments no longer make an important difference. For creatures as flexible and as dependent on learning as human beings, that seems like a particularly strong assumption.

r001.rationale: The response says heritability depends on the environments studied and that learning is flexible, but it does not attribute inconsistent genetics–trait relationships, such as for educational attainment, to the complexity of the developmental process linking genes to outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the difficulty is with that phrase “good enough.” It suggests that there’s a threshold: once you’ve provided enough food and enough stimulation, the environment has done its work, and then the genes take over. But development doesn’t seem to work that way. Genes and environments are interacting throughout the process, and children themselves are changing the environments that they experience.

There’s also a distinction between explaining variation within a particular environment and explaining what’s possible. If you make environments more similar, then genetic differences may account for a larger proportion of the differences you observe. But that doesn’t tell you what would happen if you introduced a new environment, or a new way of teaching, or a different social arrangement.

So I’m perfectly happy to think that genetic differences matter. What I doubt is the inference that, once we’ve removed certain obvious disadvantages, we’ve somehow reached the limits of what changing environments can do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says genes and environments interact throughout development, but does not mention inconsistent relationships between genetics and traits such as educational attainment or attribute that lack of consistency to developmental complexity.
